record.ear: Fair and cold. High 31. Low 20. Thaw expected Monday.

lead.headline: Chicago coroner's jury hears the Clark Street garage record in open session
lead.deck: Coroner Bundesen overrules the owner's counsel at 2:05 p.m.; record of 14 minutes 20 seconds played once to six jurors standing; voices not identified; inquest adjourned to March
lead.body: Coroner Herman N. Bundesen overruled at 2:05 p.m. yesterday the motion of the building owner's counsel that the record of the Clark Street garage be heard in private, and ordered it played in open session. The record, of 14 minutes 20 seconds, was played once to the six jurors, who heard it standing. The Coroner said the voices on it 'are not yet identified by anyone in this room.' The inquest is adjourned to a date in March. No arrests have been made.

columns.headline: Jamaica marathon ends at 243 hours; the judges rule Monday
columns.body: The last couple on the Jamaica Arena floor, Mr. and Mrs. Walter Dunn of Ozone Park, left it at 11:52 p.m. yesterday, after 243 hours 50 minutes. Mrs. Margaret Corrigan danced alone until the records were stopped at 12:30 a.m. The judges rule on Monday.

columns.headline: Week's count: harvest closed by the thaw at 88,900 tons, 1,100 short
columns.body: The Bowery Bay company closed the Sound harvest on Thursday at 88,900 tons, 1,100 tons short of last summer's use, the thaw having rotted the Whitestone field to five inches. Mr. Owen Pratt says the companies will 'make it up in price, or in sawdust.'

columns.headline: Byrd's ships to sail north from the Bay of Whales on Tuesday
columns.body: Commander Byrd's operator reported last night that the City of New York and the Eleanor Bolling will sail from the Bay of Whales on Tuesday, leaving 42 men at Little America for the winter. The message was played at 10 in the Record's window to 340.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Mr. Francis Gorman filed notice of appeal from Justice Rourke's order at 4:40 p.m. yesterday.

speaker.ear: Fair and cold. High 31. Jamaica's feet are going home to bed.

lead.headline: Marathon winds down at last, but the record won't
lead.deck: Two hundred and forty-three hours, fifty minutes; the Dunns of Ozone Park sit down at eight to midnight; Mrs. Corrigan keeps going till the management switches the band off
lead.body: At eight minutes to midnight last night, Mr. and Mrs. Walter Dunn of Ozone Park sat down on the floor of the Jamaica Arena, two hundred and forty-three hours after they stood up on it, and did not get up again. That left Mrs. Corrigan of Hollis waltzing to the Harmony Kings for the forty-first time. At half past twelve the management switched the band off. She asked them to put it back on. The judges will say on Monday who has won. The Kings have still not noticed.

columns.headline: Chicago's inquest takes the garage record off the hook and into open court
columns.body: Coroner Bundesen ruled yesterday that the Clark Street garage record be played in open session, and six jurors stood to hear it. It runs fourteen minutes. We have not heard it and will not describe it. The voices on it have not yet been put to names.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Who takes the marathon prize?'
columns.body: Madam, the operator does not judge dances. She notes, however, that the band played every minute of the two hundred and forty-three hours without one wrong note or one complaint, and that nobody has proposed giving the prize to the band.

columns.headline: Where's WORS? Eighty-one pins, and the wall is getting crowded
columns.body: Two more readers wrote this week, one from a barge at Newtown Creek and one from a Bayside attic, and the map now carries eighty-one pins. Mr. Pike of the Radio Division has his own box of pins. He has not yet put one in.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Gorman has appealed the eleven seconds. The Board says it will be glad to say nothing again, higher up.

editorial.headline: Lilith sends the editor a valentine
editorial.body: On St. Valentine's Day this editor found upon his desk a card of black lace cut in the shape of a spider, and inside it the words: To Barnaby, who reads every word I write. We print it to show the borough what it is dealing with: a woman with the brazenness to make sport of a public man in his own office. Our readers' letters this week call the valentine 'charming,' 'witty' and, from a Mrs. Gorski of Dutch Kills, 'more than he deserves.' We remind Mrs. Gorski that in Chicago this week a garage heard its own massacre and the police have subpoenaed the record. Some of us still take crime seriously. Some of us sweep it under a doily.

record.ear: Cloudy and milder. High 38. Low 29. Rain Monday.

lead.headline: Diocese asks the faithful to keep 'the custody of the ears' through Lent
lead.deck: Lenten pastoral letter to be read at all Masses this morning; householders asked to silence the house system one hour each evening; operators 'not bound'
lead.body: A Lenten pastoral letter of the Diocese of Brooklyn will be read at all Masses this morning, the Chancery announced last night. The letter asks the faithful to keep 'the custody of the ears' through Lent, to switch off the listening system of the house for one hour each evening, and 'to hear nothing that is not theirs to hear.' It states that telephone operators, 'who hear by their duty,' are not bound by the request. The letter runs to 1,140 words.

columns.headline: Steinway church reads by telephone a fifth Sunday; fourth for a valve
columns.body: Members of the First Reformed Church of Steinway read the sermon by telephone today to its 212 shut-ins for a fifth Sunday. The Newark works resumed making on Monday; the church is fourth on its list for a fifty-watt output valve, the Rev. Martin Ostrander says.

columns.headline: Lasko trial opens tomorrow; Judge Conklin to rule first on the parlour record
columns.body: Judge Conklin will rule at 10 tomorrow in the County Court, Long Island City, on Mr. Saul Feder's motion to exclude the Hale parlour record, and will then draw the jury in the trial of Mr. Victor Lasko. The fur coat has not been found.

columns.headline: Carters count 21 horses down on ice since December; four under the elevated
columns.body: Twenty-one horses have fallen on ice in Queens since December 1, the Long Island City carters' association reports, four of them under the elevated on Roosevelt Avenue, where water drips from the structure and freezes. The association has written to the Transit Commission.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Little America reported 'loading the ships, 11 below, the pups aboard for a visit' at 9:45 p.m.

speaker.ear: Milder. High 38. Sunday, and Lent. Give something up. Not the Speaker.

lead.headline: Diocese asks Queens to hang up on the house for an hour a night in Lent
lead.deck: The pastoral letter wants the system switched off each evening and the ears kept in custody; operators excused, being paid to hear
lead.body: This morning in thirty-eight Queens churches the faithful will be asked to give up, for Lent, the one thing nobody in Queens has ever given up: listening. One hour a night, the letter says, switch off the house. Hear nothing that is not yours. The operators are excused, since they hear for a living, and one of them told us she would gladly give it up if the Diocese would take her switchboard for forty days. Several landlords have asked whether the letter applies to landlords. It does.

columns.headline: The Listening Lady: Forest Hills gives up eavesdropping, from nine to ten
columns.body: Darlings, a Forest Hills hostess has resolved to switch off her house from nine to ten each night for Lent, and has invited eleven friends to do it with her, at her house, so that she can hear whether they do.

columns.headline: Feder and the parlour face off tomorrow, and the judge holds the switch
columns.body: Judge Conklin rules at ten tomorrow whether the Hale parlour may testify against Mr. Lasko, then draws the jury. Mr. Feder says the parlour is a hearsay witness with a good memory. The District Attorney says it is the only witness who stayed awake.

columns.headline: The El drips on the horses, and the carters say it's beneath them
columns.body: Twenty-one horses down on the ice since December, four under the elevated on Roosevelt Avenue, where the structure drips and the drip freezes. The carters have written to the Transit Commission. The horses have not been consulted, though they have opinions.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Byrd's pups have been taken aboard ship to say goodbye. Jackson bit a sailor. We are proud.

record.ear: Rain. High 42. Low 34. Fog on the river by night.

lead.headline: Assemblyman Burkhardt cites the Chicago garage record for his Listening Act
lead.deck: Statement at Albany yesterday; an amendment to admit records of a death in any proceeding; Mr. Ambrose Tully replies that the record 'convicts the building'; third reading March 5
lead.body: Assemblyman Burkhardt, sponsor of the Listening Act, said in a statement at Albany yesterday that the Chicago coroner's hearing of the Clark Street garage record 'shows what a room can tell a jury, and what our courts may not yet hear.' He will offer an amendment admitting records of a death in any proceeding. Mr. Ambrose Tully, for the Real Estate Owners' Association, replied that the record 'convicts the building.' The Act's third reading is set for March 5. The voice heard in the gallery on January 22 remains unidentified.

columns.headline: Athletic Club five beat the Paterson Crescents 31 to 27 before 1,600
columns.body: The Long Island City Athletic Club five beat the Paterson Crescents 31 to 27 at the armory on Saturday night before 1,600, Mr. Frank Dillon scoring 14. The club stands at ten wins and six losses. The game was broadcast to St. John's Hospital a third time.

columns.headline: Judge Conklin rules at 10 on the Hale parlour record; jury to be drawn
columns.body: Judge Conklin will give his decision at 10 this morning on Mr. Saul Feder's motion to exclude the parlour record of the Hale house, and the drawing of a jury in the trial of Mr. Victor Lasko will follow. Detective Sergeant Edward Moran will be the first witness.

columns.headline: First new Newark sleeves reach Queens counters today at 1 dollar 10
columns.body: The first receiving valves made at the Newark works since the January fire reach Queens counters this morning at 1 dollar 10 the sleeve, the company states, 1,800 sleeves in the first truck. The Arcade's hardware counter has orders for 340. Eggs are 50 cents.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: The Jamaica marathon judges will announce the award at the Arena at noon.

speaker.ear: Rain. High 42. The parlour is in court today. Wipe your feet.

lead.headline: Judge puts the parlour on the stand, and Lasko goes on the record
lead.deck: Conklin denies Feder's motion at four minutes past ten; twelve men drawn by twenty to five; the Hale house will be heard on Wednesday
lead.body: At four minutes past ten this morning Judge Conklin denied Mr. Feder's motion and ruled that the parlour of the Hale house may testify. The law in Albany is unsettled, he said, but the law in his courtroom is not, and a room is a witness 'when it is the only one present.' By twenty to five twelve men were in the box, every one of them asked whether his own house listens. Eleven said yes. One said he had never asked it. The parlour will be heard on Wednesday.

columns.headline: Club five tune up on Paterson, and St. John's stays on the line
columns.body: The Athletic Club five beat the Paterson Crescents 31 to 27 on Saturday, Dillon fourteen, ten and six for the season. St. John's heard it on the air again. The patients now send the team a written report on each game, with marks out of ten.

columns.headline: The Dunns take the prize, and Mrs. Corrigan takes the record home
columns.body: At noon the judges awarded the thousand dollars to Mr. and Mrs. Dunn of Ozone Park, the last couple standing, and the management, by way of consolation, gave Mrs. Corrigan of Hollis the Harmony Kings' six hours on copper. She says she will never play them.

columns.headline: Burkhardt puts Chicago on the line, and Tully hangs up on him
columns.body: Assemblyman Burkhardt says Chicago's garage record proves a room can tell a jury what happened. Mr. Tully of the landlords says it proves only that the building is guilty, and wonders aloud what sentence a garage receives. Albany votes on the Act on March 5.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: The new Newark valves reached the Arcade at nine. By ten Queens was talking louder. Coincidence, says Newark.

record.ear: Clearing and colder. High 36. Low 25. Northwest wind.

lead.headline: Judge Conklin admits the Hale parlour record; Lasko jury sworn at 4:40 p.m.
lead.deck: Motion to exclude denied at 10:04 a.m.; 'a room is a witness when it is the only one present'; 56 talesmen examined; the record to be played Wednesday
lead.body: Judge Conklin denied at 10:04 a.m. yesterday Mr. Saul Feder's motion to exclude the parlour record of the Hale house of Christmas Eve, holding that 'a room is a witness when it is the only one present.' Mr. Feder took exception. Fifty-six talesmen were examined, each asked whether his house had a listening system; a jury of twelve was sworn at 4:40 p.m. Detective Sergeant Edward Moran will be heard this morning and the record, of two hours ten minutes, on Wednesday. The fur coat has not been found.

columns.headline: Hallett's Point Ice Company offers summer contracts at 35 cents
columns.body: The Hallett's Point Ice Company of Astoria offered householders yesterday summer contracts for ice at 35 cents the hundredweight, delivered, against last summer's 45. The Bowery Bay company, which holds most of the harvest, said it 'will not follow a price into the river.'

columns.headline: Marathon prize of 1,000 dollars awarded to Mr. and Mrs. Walter Dunn
columns.body: The judges of the Jamaica Arena marathon awarded the prize of 1,000 dollars at noon yesterday to Mr. and Mrs. Walter Dunn of Ozone Park. The management presented Mrs. Margaret Corrigan of Hollis with the records of the Harmony Kings orchestra played during the contest.

columns.headline: First Newark sleeves sold out at the Arcade by 2:15 p.m.
columns.body: The Vantry Arcade's hardware counter sold its first 340 sleeves of new Newark valves by 2:15 p.m. yesterday at 1 dollar 10, the counterman reports, with no limit. Used valves fell to 30 cents on Jackson Avenue. Eggs are 49 cents.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: The City of New York and the Eleanor Bolling sail from the Bay of Whales at noon today, local time, Commander Byrd's operator reports.

columns.headline: Interborough states that its Corona line has the stations shown on its maps
columns.body: The Interborough Rapid Transit Company stated yesterday, in reply to a letter from the Transit Commission, that the Corona line has the stations shown on its published maps and no others. The Commission had not asked about others. The company adds that Motorman Havlik has returned to duty on the Astoria line.

columns.headline: Homing club keeps the extra bird after no owner comes forward
columns.body: The Maspeth Homing Club has entered the blue bar hen with the 'Loft 9' band in its own book, no owner having replied to 140 letters. She has now flown with the club four times and has come home first on three of them, from a direction which the secretary states he is unable to account for.

columns.headline: Sanitation finds Corona heaps in order; no complaint on file
columns.body: The Department of Sanitation reports that an inspector visited the Corona ash dumps on Saturday and found the north heaps sorted by material, to a height of about nine feet, with a clear path between them. The Department has no complaint on file, as none has been made. The inspector was not asked to return.

columns.headline: Society for the Prevention: subscriptions now due
columns.body: Members of the Society for the Prevention are reminded that subscriptions fall due with the March meeting. The officers report that the year has so far been quiet, as intended. Correspondence will not be answered. Address Box 1871, the Record.

back.foot: The Borough Record. Printed at Long Island City.

speaker.ear: Colder. High 36. Ice at 35 cents. Get it while it's hot.

lead.headline: Ice war breaks out on the Sound, and summer prices skate on thin ice
lead.deck: Hallett's Point offers 35 cents the hundredweight; Bowery Bay won't follow it into the river; a householder can now save a dime by July and lose it by August
lead.body: The ice business, which has been cold all winter, has finally heated up. Hallett's Point of Astoria, which holds the smaller house and the louder salesman, is offering summer ice at thirty-five cents the hundredweight, ten under last year. Bowery Bay, with most of the harvest and Mr. Pratt, says it will not follow a price into the river. Mr. Pratt has spent three months praying for cold. He is now praying for a hot July and a short memory. Sign nothing until Saturday, we say. Somebody will blink.

columns.headline: Sergeant Moran opens for the people, and the parlour clears its throat
columns.body: Sergeant Moran told the jury this morning how he found Mr. Lasko in Corona after Christmas, and what he did not find, which was the coat. Mr. Feder asked him about a lineman's string. The judge asked what string. The parlour is heard tomorrow.

columns.headline: Newark's new valves sell out by a quarter past two, and Queens turns it up
columns.body: The Arcade's first three hundred and forty new sleeves were gone by a quarter past two, at a dollar ten and no limit. The pawnbroker on Jackson Avenue has marked his used valves to thirty cents and is looking for another line of work.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Why don't the ice men use the telephone?'
columns.body: Sir, they do, but only in winter, when they want ice to be cold, and in summer, when they want it to be dear. In between they use a horse and a bell. The operator recommends the bell. It does not ask her to hold.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Byrd's ships sail for home at noon, Antarctic time. Jackson the pup stays behind. He has a job.

lead.headline: Greenpoint householders report the Hum; Brooklyn Borough Hall says it has none
lead.deck: Petition of 64 names; tone heard 'since Saturday night' between midnight and 4 a.m.; the Borough President's engineer: 'There is no hum in Kings County'
lead.body: Sixty-four householders of Greenpoint, Brooklyn, petitioned the Brooklyn Borough President yesterday, stating that a low tone 'like the one complained of in Queens' has been heard in their houses since Saturday night, chiefly between midnight and 4 a.m. It is the first such complaint from Brooklyn. The Borough President's engineer, Mr. Clement Haig, stated at 3 p.m. that 'there is no hum in Kings County' and that the petitioners 'live near Queens.' Alderman Feeney has asked Dr. Emil Rastin to take a reading at the Greenpoint Avenue bridge.

columns.headline: Sergeant Moran's testimony opens the Lasko trial; the record today
columns.body: Detective Sergeant Edward Moran testified for two hours yesterday in the trial of Mr. Victor Lasko, describing the arrest at Corona. On cross-examination Mr. Saul Feder asked about waxed lacing cord; Judge Conklin sustained the objection. The Hale parlour record will be played at 10 today.

columns.headline: Byrd's ships leave the Bay of Whales; 42 men remain at Little America
columns.body: The City of New York and the Eleanor Bolling left the Bay of Whales at noon yesterday, local time, Commander Byrd's operator reported at 9:50 p.m., leaving 42 men at Little America for the winter. The sun now sets there for six hours of each day.

columns.headline: Whitestone company cuts summer ice to 32 cents; Bowery Bay silent
columns.body: The Whitestone Ice Company offered summer contracts yesterday at 32 cents the hundredweight, three below the Hallett's Point price of Monday. The Bowery Bay company made no statement. Mr. Owen Pratt was seen at 4 p.m. at the Whitestone company's office, and left at 4:40.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Mr. Clement Haig of the Brooklyn Borough President's office said at 9 p.m. that he had 'listened at Greenpoint and heard Queens.'

speaker.ear: Fair and cold. High 33. Brooklyn has something to tell Queens. Brooklyn would rather not.

lead.headline: Brooklyn hears the Hum, and Borough Hall says it's a wrong number
lead.deck: Sixty-four Greenpoint householders complain of a tone after midnight; Brooklyn's engineer says there is no hum in Kings County, only people who live too near Queens
lead.body: For three months Brooklyn has read about the Hum the way a man reads about another man's toothache. Since Saturday, sixty-four householders of Greenpoint say, they have had it too, between midnight and four, low, like ours. Brooklyn's Borough Hall has answered them. There is no hum in Kings County, says its engineer, Mr. Haig. The petitioners merely live near Queens. Greenpoint, which has been told many things in its time, has never before been told it lives in the wrong borough. Dr. Rastin is bringing his meter.

columns.headline: The Hale parlour has its say for two hours ten, and the jury leans in
columns.body: The Hale parlour had its say this morning, two hours and ten minutes of Christmas Eve, mostly a clock and a dog asleep. At the fifty-first minute the jury heard a window. Mr. Lasko looked at his shoes. Mr. Feder took a great many notes.

columns.headline: Ice war: Whitestone cuts to thirty-two, and Pratt pays a cool call
columns.body: Whitestone has cut summer ice to thirty-two cents, three under Hallett's Point. Mr. Pratt of Bowery Bay was seen going into the Whitestone office at four and coming out at twenty to five, and neither side will say what was said. We would pay well for that room's record.

columns.headline: Where's WORS? A Greenpoint reader sends pin eighty-two from across the creek
columns.body: For the first time a reader in Brooklyn has written to say she heard WORS, at the end of Kingsland Avenue, on Sunday at two in the morning. Pin eighty-two goes in on the far side of Newtown Creek. Brooklyn's Borough Hall says it heard nothing.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Mr. Haig went to Greenpoint at nine to listen. He says he heard Queens. Queens says it was not talking.

record.ear: Cloudy, light snow by evening. High 31. Low 24.

lead.headline: Hale parlour record played to the Lasko jury; a window heard at the 51st minute
lead.deck: Two hours ten minutes heard in full from 10:02 a.m.; a man's voice speaks four words; Mr. Leonard Hale identifies his clock, his dog and 'not the window'
lead.body: The parlour record of the Hale house in Jackson Heights, made on Christmas Eve, was played in full to the jury in the trial of Mr. Victor Lasko from 10:02 a.m. yesterday. At the 51st minute a sash window is heard raised, followed by footsteps on the carpet for six minutes and a man's voice saying four words, which the District Attorney's clerk read into the record as 'Not this one either.' Mr. Leonard Hale identified his clock and his dog. Mr. Feder will cross-examine him today.

columns.headline: Farewell Address to be read at Borough Hall tomorrow and recorded
columns.body: The Borough President's office states that President Washington's Farewell Address will be read in full from the steps of Borough Hall at noon tomorrow by Judge Lemuel Archer of the Municipal Court, and recorded for the Phonautograph Society. The reading is expected to take 45 minutes.

columns.headline: Dr. Rastin reads 41 cycles at the Greenpoint Avenue bridge, Brooklyn side
columns.body: Dr. Emil Rastin of Columbia took a reading at the Brooklyn end of the Greenpoint Avenue bridge at 1:20 a.m. yesterday, at Alderman Feeney's request. His meter read 41 cycles. Mr. Clement Haig, of the Brooklyn Borough President's office, stated that the reading 'was taken facing Queens.'

columns.headline: Senator Harlan declines to play the Chicago record to his committee
columns.body: Senator Edmund Harlan, chairman of the Judiciary Committee, yesterday declined Assemblyman Burkhardt's request that a copy of the Clark Street garage record be played to the committee, stating that 'the State of New York does not need to hear Chicago to know its own mind.'

record.wire: LATE WIRE: A mare of the Corona Ice Company fell under the elevated on Roosevelt Avenue at 7:10 p.m. and lay 50 minutes before rising.

speaker.ear: Snow by evening. High 31. Watch your step under the El. Ask any horse.

lead.headline: Ice mare goes down under the El, and the carters get on their high horse
lead.deck: Biddy of the Corona Ice Company lies fifty minutes on Roosevelt Avenue in the drip; the carters meet tonight in Woodside, and the Transit Commission is invited
lead.body: At ten past seven last night Biddy, a grey mare of the Corona Ice Company, went down on Roosevelt Avenue under the elevated, where the structure drips and the drip freezes, and lay on the ice for fifty minutes while her driver, two patrolmen and a trolley crew put sacks and ashes under her. She got up. She will not work for a week, which in her trade is a holiday. She is the twenty-second horse down this winter. The carters meet tonight in Woodside.

columns.headline: Feder asks Mr. Hale whose voice it was, and the parlour isn't saying
columns.body: Mr. Feder spent the morning asking Mr. Hale whether the four words on his parlour record were Mr. Lasko's. Mr. Hale said he could not say, never having spoken with Mr. Lasko. Mr. Feder said that was his point. The judge said it was a short point, made at length.

columns.headline: Brooklyn tunes out: Rastin reads forty-one, and Haig says he faced wrong
columns.body: Dr. Rastin stood on the Brooklyn end of the Greenpoint Avenue bridge at twenty past one yesterday morning and read forty-one. Mr. Haig of Brooklyn says the doctor was facing Queens. The doctor says the meter does not face anything. Brooklyn is considering this.

columns.headline: Washington says goodbye at Borough Hall tomorrow, long distance
columns.body: Judge Archer reads the Farewell Address from the Borough Hall steps at noon tomorrow, all forty-five minutes of it, and the Phonautograph Society records the lot. It is the longest goodbye in American history. The operators say they have heard longer, most Sundays.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Biddy has eaten a full nosebag. Her driver has not. The carters' meeting begins at eight.

record.ear: Snow, two inches, ending by morning. High 30. Low 21. Washington's Birthday; banks and post office closed.

lead.headline: Carters ask the Transit Commission to sand Roosevelt Avenue below the elevated
lead.deck: Three hundred and ten carters at Woodside Hall until 11:20 p.m.; the Corona Ice Company's mare the 22nd horse down since December; no deliveries beneath the structure after March 15
lead.body: Three hundred and ten carters met at Woodside Hall last night until 11:20 p.m. and resolved to ask the Transit Commission to sand Roosevelt Avenue beneath the elevated each morning before 6, and to repair the structure's drip. The meeting was called after a grey mare of the Corona Ice Company fell beneath the elevated on Wednesday evening, the 22nd horse down in Queens since December. If no answer is received by March 15, the carters will not deliver beneath the structure. The Commission's engineer did not attend.

columns.headline: Farewell Address to be read at noon today; Borough Hall closed to business
columns.body: Judge Lemuel Archer of the Municipal Court will read President Washington's Farewell Address from the steps of Borough Hall at noon today, the 197th anniversary of his birth. The reading will be recorded by the Phonautograph Society. Banks, the post office and the Stock Exchange are closed.

columns.headline: Mr. Hale 'could not say' whose voice; the People rest in the Lasko trial
columns.body: Mr. Leonard Hale was cross-examined for 2 hours 20 minutes yesterday by Mr. Saul Feder, and said he 'could not say' whose voice spoke the four words on his parlour record. The People rested at 3:50 p.m. Mr. Feder opens the defence on Monday.

columns.headline: Brooklyn Borough President's office declines to hear Greenpoint petitioners
columns.body: The Brooklyn Borough President's office yesterday declined a hearing to the 64 Greenpoint petitioners, Mr. Clement Haig stating that the matter 'belongs to the Public Service Commission and to Queens.' Commissioner Lacey gives his decision on the Queens petition on Tuesday at 10.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: The Bowery Bay company announced at 10 p.m. summer contracts at 30 cents the hundredweight.

speaker.ear: Snow ended. High 30. Washington's Birthday. Tell the truth today; it's traditional.

lead.headline: Washington's farewell runs forty-four minutes, and Queens stays on the line
lead.deck: Judge Archer reads the whole goodbye from the Borough Hall steps in two inches of snow; fourteen hundred listen; the Society takes it down for 1978
lead.body: At noon Judge Lemuel Archer of the Municipal Court stood on the steps of Borough Hall in two inches of snow and read the first President's Farewell Address to fourteen hundred people and the Phonautograph Society's machine. It took forty-four minutes. The General warned against faction, foreign entanglement and excessive party spirit. Queens stamped its feet and listened anyway. Nobody left, which Judge Archer says is more than he gets at the Municipal Court. In 1978 they can hear it. We hope they listen better than we do.

columns.headline: Carters rein in the El: sand by six, or no ice under the tracks
columns.body: Three hundred and ten carters met in Woodside last night and gave the Transit Commission until March 15 to sand Roosevelt Avenue and stop the drip. After that, no ice and no coal will be carried under the elevated. The El has not replied. It is dripping.

columns.headline: Ice war: Bowery Bay drops to thirty, and the Sound goes into a price freeze
columns.body: Mr. Pratt has spoken. Bowery Bay will deliver all summer at thirty cents the hundredweight, under Whitestone and Hallett's Point both. He says he has the ice and they have the salesmen. Queens has never been so cheaply cooled, on paper. July will tell.

columns.headline: Brooklyn won't take the call, and Greenpoint is put through to Queens
columns.body: Brooklyn's Borough Hall has refused the Greenpoint petitioners a hearing and told them the Hum belongs to Queens and the Commission. Greenpoint says it does not want the Hum, it merely has it. Commissioner Lacey rules on Tuesday. Greenpoint will be listening.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: The General's address has been given to the Society for the 1978 case. It will be filed under goodbyes.

lead.headline: Farewell Address read at Borough Hall in 44 minutes; record to the 1978 case
lead.deck: Judge Archer reads from noon to 12:44 p.m. to about 1,400 in two inches of snow; the reading 'without omission'; three masters to the Phonautograph Society
lead.body: Judge Lemuel Archer of the Municipal Court read President Washington's Farewell Address from the steps of Borough Hall at noon yesterday, without omission, to about 1,400 persons standing in two inches of snow. The reading ran 44 minutes 10 seconds. It was recorded on three masters by the Phonautograph Society of Queens, and Mr. Cyril Abbot said they will go into the fifth copper case for 1978. The Borough President stood throughout. Two persons were treated for cold. The flag was at full staff.

columns.headline: Week's count: 6,300 summer ice contracts signed at 30 to 35 cents
columns.body: The three Sound companies and Hallett's Point signed 6,300 summer contracts for household ice in the week to last night, the Bowery Bay company reports, at prices from 30 to 35 cents the hundredweight. Last year's contracts were 45 cents. Mr. Owen Pratt says the price 'will hold.'

columns.headline: Sorrentino and Lusk meet in ten rounds at Ridgewood Grove tonight
columns.body: Kid Sorrentino of Astoria and Harry Lusk of Jersey City meet in ten rounds at Ridgewood Grove tonight, the main bout at 10. The promoter states that the bout will be recorded 'at the ringside and at the ring.' Mr. Lusk weighed 141, Sorrentino 139 1/2.

columns.headline: Steel screws on the third lien notice found to be of a Vantry & Co. pattern
columns.body: Mr. Ludwig Haas removed one of the four steel screws from the third lien notice on the Arcade's north door yesterday for examination. The Borough's hardware inspector reports it to be of a Vantry & Co. pattern 'not made since 1924.' The screw was replaced at 3 p.m.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: A fifth parcel for 'Party Line, Queens Exchange, Position 43' was delivered at 4:30 p.m., postmarked Corona.

speaker.ear: Fair and cold. High 29. Party Line has mail. Again.

lead.headline: Party Line's fifth tin arrives, and Sergeant Moran is tied up in knots
lead.deck: Corona postmark, sardines, lacing cord; the exchange cat eats first and asks questions never; the Sergeant takes the string to the 104th
lead.body: At half past four yesterday the parcel post brought the fifth tin of sardines to Party Line, the exchange cat of Position 43, postmarked Corona and tied, as the fourth was, with a lineman's waxed lacing cord. Party Line ate the sardines. Sergeant Moran took the cord to the 104th Precinct, where a lineman's tool bag has been waiting since January for an owner who has not come back for it. He has not said what he found. Party Line has not asked.

columns.headline: Sorrentino and Lusk ring the bell again tonight, and round seven gets a retake
columns.body: Kid Sorrentino and Harry Lusk go ten rounds at Ridgewood Grove tonight, and the promoter will record from ringside and from the ring itself, so that the seventh round, should there be one, can be argued about properly. Lusk's manager has brought his own recording set.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Is the Hum coming to Brooklyn?'
columns.body: Madam, the operator puts through calls between Queens and Brooklyn all day, and she says the Hum, if there is one, does not need her to connect it. Brooklyn's Borough Hall says there is none. Brooklyn's Borough Hall is a long way from Greenpoint.

columns.headline: A screw loose on the Arcade door turns out older than the notice
columns.body: Mr. Haas unscrewed one of the steel screws on his third lien notice yesterday and had it looked at. It is a Vantry & Co. screw, of a pattern nobody has made since 1924. He put it back. Signal Ground Rents still does not answer the telephone.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Sixty-three hundred families signed for cheap ice this week. The ice men are shaking hands with the weather again.

editorial.headline: An Inspector's rent is his own business
editorial.body: Inspector Leonard Quill of the vice squad, who has arrested four hundred women this winter for loitering, was relieved of duty on Washington's Birthday after a parcel of his rent books was found tied to the statue of the first President in the park, with a sign: I cannot tell a lie, but he can. The books show the Inspector collecting rent from eleven houses he was paid to close. This paper will say what nobody else has the backbone to say. A policeman is entitled to invest. The women he arrested were loitering; he was merely collecting. Lilith knew his books were in his desk, and that, readers, is the true scandal: how did she know which drawer?

lead.headline: Ships clear of the pack; 42 men begin the winter alone at Little America
lead.deck: City of New York and Eleanor Bolling report at 9:30 p.m.; Commander Byrd's operator: 'the camp is alone now and well'; 58 days to the sun's last setting
lead.body: The City of New York and the Eleanor Bolling reported at 9:30 p.m. yesterday that they were clear of the Ross Sea pack and steaming north for New Zealand. Commander Byrd's operator at Little America sent at 9:52 p.m. that 'the camp is alone now and well,' with 42 men, the dogs and the pup Jackson. The sun will set at Little America for the last time on April 22 and will not rise again until August. The message was played in the Record's window to 410.

columns.headline: Sorrentino outpoints Lusk in ten rounds at Ridgewood Grove
columns.body: Kid Sorrentino of Astoria won a decision over Harry Lusk of Jersey City in ten rounds at Ridgewood Grove last night before 3,800. Both men were standing at the seventh round's bell. Mr. Lusk's manager has asked for no record.

columns.headline: Steinway church receives its output valve; sermon broadcast this morning
columns.body: The First Reformed Church of Steinway received a fifty-watt output valve from the Newark works yesterday at 2:10 p.m., and will broadcast the Rev. Martin Ostrander's sermon this morning at 11 for the first time since December. Members are thanked for five Sundays by telephone.

columns.headline: Fifth parcel for the exchange cat; cord compared with articles at the 104th
columns.body: A fifth parcel for 'Party Line, Queens Exchange, Position 43,' postmarked Corona and containing sardines, was delivered on Friday, tied with waxed lacing cord. Detective Sergeant Edward Moran compared the cord yesterday with cord in a tool bag held at the 104th Precinct. He made no statement.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: The 104th Precinct states that the tool bag of Mr. Joseph Marchetti remains in its property room, unclaimed.

speaker.ear: Milder. High 37. Sunday. Steinway's on the air. Hang up your telephones.

lead.headline: Byrd's ships sail home, and forty-two men go on the longest hold in the world
lead.deck: The last ship's wire from the pack ice at half past nine; the camp signs on alone; the sun leaves in April and comes back in August, like a lodger
lead.body: Last night the two ships that took Commander Byrd to the bottom of the world reported themselves clear of the ice and pointed for home. That leaves forty-two men, the dogs and a pup called Jackson at Little America, in huts under the snow, with a radio house and a long night coming. The sun goes on the twenty-second of April and does not come back until August. Their operator signed off: alone now and well. We will be at the Record's window every night. Somebody should be.

columns.headline: Sorrentino goes the distance, and Lusk's manager wants it off the record
columns.body: Kid Sorrentino beat Harry Lusk on points at Ridgewood Grove last night, ten rounds, both men upright at the bell of every one, including the seventh. Lusk's manager has asked for no record of any of it. Astoria is calling it the quietest win in years.

columns.headline: Steinway gets its valve, and the Reverend gets his reception back
columns.body: The First Reformed Church of Steinway had its new fifty-watt valve in by Saturday tea and Mr. Ostrander's sermon on the air this morning at eleven. The shut-ins heard him without being rung. Several rang anyway, out of habit, to say it was very good.

columns.headline: Where's WORS? Pike takes three bearings, and the lines still won't meet
columns.body: Mr. Pike of the Radio Division had three launches out this time, off Hell Gate, College Point and Riker's Island, when WORS came on at ten past two on Friday morning. He took three bearings. All three run parallel. The instruments are correct. So is the map.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Jackson the pup was heard on the Little America wire, barking. The first dog to broadcast from the Antarctic. Probably.

lead.headline: Third Radio Division bearing on WORS 1610 runs parallel with the first two
lead.deck: Launches off Hell Gate, College Point and Riker's Island receive 44 seconds at 2:10 a.m. Friday; bearings 'within half a degree of one another'; Mr. Pike 'will try a fourth'
lead.body: Mr. Harold Pike of the Radio Division reported yesterday that three of the Division's launches, stationed off Hell Gate, College Point and Riker's Island, received WORS 1610 at 2:10 a.m. on Friday for 44 seconds and each fixed a bearing. Plotted on the Coast Survey chart, the three bearings run within half a degree of one another and do not meet. The instruments were checked on Saturday and found correct. Mr. Pike said the Division 'will try a fourth.' The transmission contained a man's voice reading figures.

columns.headline: Athletic Club five lose to the Jersey City Reds 33 to 30 in an extra period
columns.body: The Long Island City Athletic Club five lost to the Jersey City Reds 33 to 30 in an extra period at the armory on Saturday night before 1,900. Mr. Frank Dillon scored 16. The club stands at ten wins and seven losses, with three games to play.

columns.headline: Mr. Feder opens the defence of Mr. Lasko this morning
columns.body: Mr. Saul Feder will open the defence in the trial of Mr. Victor Lasko at 10 this morning in the County Court. He has listed seven witnesses, among them an installer of listening systems and the defendant. The fur coat has not been found.

columns.headline: Commissioner Lacey to give decision on the Hum and the rate at 10 tomorrow
columns.body: Commissioner Maurice Lacey will give his decision at 10 tomorrow on the Astoria petition concerning the Hum and on Queens Light & Power's application for a 7 1/2-cent rate. The Greenpoint petitioners have asked to be heard and have been told the record is closed.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: The Jamaica Arena announces a second dance marathon for April, to live music, 'by request of the first.'

speaker.ear: Cloudy. High 40. Rain tomorrow, and a ruling on the Hum. Bring an umbrella.

lead.headline: Feder's defence plugs in the man who wired the Hale parlour
lead.deck: Mr. Otto Brandt of Sunnyside installed the Hale system in 1914 and says a parlour of that make has a good ear and a bad memory; Lasko testifies tomorrow
lead.body: Mr. Feder opened for the defence this morning with a small grey man named Otto Brandt, of Sunnyside, who wired the Hale parlour in 1914. A parlour of that make, Mr. Brandt told the jury, has a good ear and a bad memory, and in cold weather the copper runs slow. Asked whether it could make up four words, he said no, but it could lose a fifth. The District Attorney asked him whose voice it was. Mr. Brandt said he only does the wiring. Mr. Lasko testifies tomorrow.

columns.headline: Reds edge the Club five in extra time, and St. John's takes it lying down
columns.body: The Jersey City Reds beat the Athletic Club five 33 to 30 on Saturday in an extra period, Dillon sixteen. The patients at St. John's, listening on the air, took it lying down, which is their custom. Ten and seven, three to play.

columns.headline: Lacey rules tomorrow, and the Hum has nothing to say in its own defence
columns.body: Commissioner Lacey gives his ruling on the Hum and the light company's rate at ten tomorrow. The company says there is no tone. Dr. Rastin says forty-one. Duke of 31st Street has been asked to wait outside this time. He has agreed, in principle.

columns.headline: Arena books a live band for the next marathon, and calls it fair play
columns.body: The Jamaica Arena will hold a second dance marathon in April, the management says, to a band of real musicians in shifts, at the written request of the first marathon's dancers. Mrs. Corrigan of Hollis has entered. She says she has unfinished business with a band.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS read out numbers on Friday morning. Mr. Pike wrote them down. He will not say if they add up.

lead.headline: Hale installer says the system 'loses words in the cold'; Lasko testifies today
lead.deck: Mr. Otto Brandt of Sunnyside, who installed it in 1914, for the defence; 'it cannot add a word, but it may lose one'; Mr. Lasko to take the stand at 10
lead.body: Mr. Otto Brandt of Sunnyside, who installed the listening system of the Hale house in 1914, testified for the defence yesterday in the trial of Mr. Victor Lasko that a system of that make 'loses words in the cold' and that 'it cannot add a word, but it may lose one.' On cross-examination he said he could not identify the voice on the parlour record. Four other defence witnesses were heard as to Mr. Lasko's character. Mr. Lasko will take the stand at 10 this morning.

columns.headline: Commissioner Lacey gives his decision on the Hum at 10 this morning
columns.body: Commissioner Maurice Lacey gives his decision at 10 this morning in Long Island City on the Astoria petition concerning the Hum, signed by 2,140 householders, and on the 7 1/2-cent rate. Alderman Feeney, Dr. Emil Rastin and Mr. Roland Tisch will attend. The terrier Duke will not.

columns.headline: Radio Division's record of WORS 1610 on Friday contains figures read aloud
columns.body: The 44 seconds of WORS 1610 received by the Radio Division's launches at 2:10 a.m. on Friday consist of a man's voice reading figures in groups of four, Mr. Harold Pike stated yesterday. He declined to publish the figures 'until they have been read correctly.'

columns.headline: Mr. Gorman's appeal on the Riverhead record set for March 18
columns.body: The Appellate Division, Second Department, will hear on March 18 Mr. Francis Gorman's appeal from Justice Thaddeus Rourke's order upholding the Board of Elections' seal on the 11 seconds of its Riverhead record. The bench warrant for Mr. Joseph Marchetti, lineman, remains outstanding.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Greenpoint householders report the tone 'as before' between midnight and 3:40 a.m.

speaker.ear: Rain. High 44. The Commission has ruled. The Hum has not been told.

lead.headline: Lacey hears both sides and rules the Hum out of order, mostly
lead.deck: Half a cent on the rate, no finding on the tone, and the company told to let a Commission engineer into Astoria by April; Duke waits outside and says nothing
lead.body: Commissioner Lacey took fifty-one minutes this morning to read his ruling, and when he had finished nobody in the room was sure who had won. The company gets seven cents, not seven and a half. The Astoria petition is dismissed, the Commissioner being unable to find a tone in the company's readings or an absence of one in Dr. Rastin's. Then he ordered the company to admit a Commission engineer to its Astoria works by April 1, with a meter not of its own make. Duke, outside, said nothing.

columns.headline: Lasko takes the stand and gives his side of the record
columns.body: Mr. Lasko told the jury this morning that on Christmas Eve he was at his sister's in Corona until one, and that the four words on the Hale record are not his. The District Attorney asked him to say them. He said them. The jury listened very hard.

columns.headline: Where's WORS? The station reads out its numbers, and Pike won't share the sum
columns.body: Friday's forty-four seconds of WORS were a man reading figures in fours, Mr. Pike says. He will not print them until they are read correctly. Our readers have sent in eleven sets of figures they say they heard. No two agree. All are pinned up.

columns.headline: Gorman's appeal gets a date, and the eleven seconds stay on hold
columns.body: The Appellate Division will hear Mr. Gorman's appeal on the Board's sealed eleven seconds on March 18. The Board says the seal is the seal. Mr. Gorman says a seal is only wax. Marchetti, who might know what is underneath it, is still not taking calls.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Greenpoint heard the tone again last night. Brooklyn's engineer says Greenpoint should face the other way.

lead.headline: Commission allows a 7-cent rate and dismisses the Astoria petition on the Hum
lead.deck: Commissioner Lacey reads for 51 minutes; no finding on the tone either way; the company to admit a Commission engineer to its Astoria works by April 1
lead.body: Commissioner Maurice Lacey yesterday allowed Queens Light & Power a rate of 7 cents, against the 7 1/2 cents applied for, and dismissed the Astoria petition concerning the Hum, stating that the Commission 'is unable to find a tone in the company's readings, or the absence of one in the petitioners' readings.' He directed the company to admit a Commission engineer, 'with an instrument not of the company's make,' to its Astoria works by April 1. Alderman Feeney said he would 'wait for April.' Mr. Roland Tisch made no statement.

columns.headline: Mr. Lasko denies the words on the Hale record; summations today
columns.body: Mr. Victor Lasko testified for 1 hour 50 minutes yesterday that he spent Christmas Eve at his sister's house in Corona until 1 a.m. At the District Attorney's request he spoke the four words on the parlour record to the jury. Summations begin at 10 today.

columns.headline: Aberystwyth acknowledges Dr. Strand's letter on the WORS 1610 carol
columns.body: Dr. Matthias Strand of Union Seminary has received from the National Library of Wales at Aberystwyth an acknowledgment of his letter of February 4 concerning the carol heard on WORS 1610. The Library 'will search its collections' and asks for a written copy of the tune.

columns.headline: Arcade toy shop finds the two returned dolls turned to face the shop
columns.body: The proprietress of the Vantry Arcade's toy shop reports that the two answering dolls returned by Mrs. Voss and Mrs. Strub, placed on the back shelf facing the wall, were found on Monday morning facing the shop. She has turned them back.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Alderman Feeney has asked to accompany the Commission's engineer into the Astoria works 'with the dog.'

speaker.ear: Colder. High 38. The light company got half a cent. Astoria got April.

lead.headline: Feder tells the jury to hang up on the parlour; the D.A. says it never lies
lead.deck: Summations at Long Island City: four words, two hours ten minutes, one window and no coat; the judge charges at a quarter to three, and the jury goes out at ten past four
lead.body: Mr. Feder spoke for an hour and forty minutes this morning and said, in short, that a room is not a man. It cannot be cross-examined, and it cannot tell you who it heard, only what. Then the District Attorney spoke for an hour and said, in shorter, that a room has no reason to lie. Nobody mentioned the coat, which has still not been found. Judge Conklin charged the jury this afternoon, and it went out at ten past four. Mr. Lasko wore the new suit again.

columns.headline: Dolls on the back shelf turn round to face the music
columns.body: The two answering dolls on the toy shop's back shelf, put there facing the wall in January, were found on Monday morning facing the shop. The proprietress turned them back. She says she is not asking them anything, and they are not to ask her.

columns.headline: Wales takes the call on the carol, and asks for the tune in writing
columns.body: The National Library of Wales has written back to Dr. Strand to say it will search its collections for the WORS carol, and would he please send the tune written down. Dr. Strand says it has never been written down. That, he says, is the trouble.

columns.headline: Feeney asks to take Duke into the works, and the company won't take the lead
columns.body: Alderman Feeney has asked to go into the Astoria works on April 1 with the Commission's engineer, and with Duke of 31st Street, on a lead. The company says the order names one engineer and one instrument. The Alderman says Duke is an instrument.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: April 1 is the day the engineer goes in. We are told this is a coincidence. We are printing it anyway.

record.ear: Fair and cold. High 34. Low 22. March comes in tomorrow.

lead.headline: Lasko jury retires at 4:10 p.m.; asks at 9:20 to hear the parlour record again
lead.deck: Judge Conklin's charge 1 hour 12 minutes; the jury locked up for the night at the Long Island City courthouse; the record to be replayed at 10 a.m.
lead.body: Judge Conklin charged the jury in the trial of Mr. Victor Lasko for 1 hour 12 minutes yesterday, instructing that the parlour record of the Hale house 'is evidence of what was heard, and not of who was heard,' and the jury retired at 4:10 p.m. At 9:20 p.m. the foreman sent a note asking that the record be played again in full. Judge Conklin ordered the jury locked up for the night and the record replayed at 10 this morning. The fur coat has not been found.

columns.headline: Listening Act on the calendar for March 5; gallery voice unidentified
columns.body: Assemblyman Thomas Burkhardt's print of the Listening Act, with his amendment admitting records of a death in any proceeding, is on the Assembly calendar for third reading on March 5. The Clerk has compared the voice heard in the gallery on January 22 with 61 visitors, without a match.

columns.headline: Month's count: valves 1 dollar 05 the sleeve; eggs 46 cents
columns.body: The sleeve of receiving valves closed the month at 1 dollar 05 at the Vantry Arcade, against 1 dollar 45 on February 1. Used valves were 25 cents on Jackson Avenue. Eggs were 46 cents, coal 15 dollars the ton, summer ice contracts 30 cents the hundredweight.

columns.headline: Phonautograph Society to meet March 8 on Mrs. Grieve's motion
columns.body: The Phonautograph Society of Queens will meet on March 8 at the Jamaica office, where Mrs. Ottoline Grieve will move a third time that record No. 23, the Maspeth party's midnight record, be played to members. Mr. Cyril Abbot has said he will again oppose.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: The Arcade's toy shop reports the two dolls on the back shelf facing the wall at closing.

speaker.ear: Fair and cold. High 34. Last day of February. March is on the other line.

lead.headline: Lasko jury asks for a replay, and spends the night with the parlour
lead.deck: Out at ten past four, a note at twenty past nine: play it again, all two hours ten; Judge Conklin locks them up and the record goes on at ten
lead.body: The Lasko jury went out at ten past four yesterday and at twenty past nine sent the judge a note. It did not say guilty and it did not say not guilty. It said: play it again. All of it, the clock, the dog, the window, the six minutes of footsteps and the four words. So this morning at ten twelve men sat down for another two hours and ten minutes of Christmas Eve in a Jackson Heights parlour. As we go to press, they are still out.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Where is the twenty-ninth of February?'
columns.body: Sir, the operator has looked, and it is not on her board this year. It is held over until 1932, like the Listening Act, only further. Should you need to speak to the twenty-ninth urgently, she suggests you hold.

columns.headline: Burkhardt's Act gets its date, and the gallery voice still won't speak up
columns.body: Albany has the Listening Act down for March 5, Chicago amendment and all. The Clerk has now had sixty-one visitors say 'resent' into his machine. None of them is the voice from the gallery. The Clerk says he is beginning to resent it himself.

columns.headline: Where's WORS? Ninety-four pins at month's end, and the lines won't connect
columns.body: February ends with ninety-four pins on the Speaker's wall, one of them in Brooklyn, and Mr. Pike's three parallel bearings drawn on in red. Our engraver has stopped asking what the map is of. Our office boy says the pins look like they are queueing.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Mrs. Grieve moves again on March 8. Mr. Abbot is said to be practising his casting vote.
